strengths: Addresses speech bandwidth extension, a relevant speech-processing problem, with an intuitively interesting proposal to incorporate nonlinear-dynamics-inspired signals into adversarial training.
Reports several complementary objective metrics, parameter counts, computational costs, and ablations over discriminator and generator choices.

The proposed discriminator modules are comparatively lightweight, and the manuscript explicitly acknowledges limitations involving single-dataset, clean-speech evaluation and untested multilingual generalization.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not adequately supported. Table 3 leaves most baseline entries blank—NU-Wave, EBEN, and AERO have no results, while MS-BWE has only two reported values—yet the text claims broad superiority over the baselines across metrics and bandwidth ranges.

The paper claims subjective evaluation with five human judges in the abstract and conclusion, but provides no listening-test protocol, stimuli counts, participant information, rating procedure, results, uncertainty, or statistical analysis. NISQA-MOS is an automatic metric and cannot substitute for the claimed human evaluation.

Essential experimental information is absent: there is no train/development/test split, speaker partition, number or duration of evaluated utterances, random seeds, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Possible speaker or utterance leakage therefore cannot be excluded.

The training objective is not specified. The manuscript omits the generator and discriminator loss functions, adversarial formulation, reconstruction losses, loss weights, and optimization schedule details needed to reproduce the system or understand what drives its results.

The nonlinear-dynamics interpretation is insufficiently validated. Speech being nonlinear does not by itself establish deterministic chaos, and the experiments do not show that the proposed features measure chaos rather than ordinary signal statistics. No direct analysis of estimated Lyapunov exponents, DFA behavior, or correspondence to perceptual improvements is provided.

The new discriminators are underspecified and technically questionable. MRLD leaves embedding dimension, delay, neighbor selection, temporal offset, normalization, boundary handling, and differentiability details undefined. MSDFA appears to tile each scalar fluctuation value into a constant image; it does not clearly estimate the DFA scaling exponent and gives no justification for why a 2-D CNN over tiled constants is appropriate.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the claimed mechanisms: configurations simultaneously change discriminator families, convolution types, scale counts, generator architecture, attention heads, and parameter counts. There are no capacity-matched conventional discriminators or simple statistical-feature controls, so improvements cannot be attributed specifically to chaos modeling.

Reported results contain inconsistencies. The abstract describes seven discriminators, including recurrence and Poincaré-plot discriminators, whereas the implemented method and final system describe four principal discriminators. Claims such as an eight-times reduction, a 40-times discriminator reduction, and a roughly two-times overall model reduction refer to different comparisons without consistently defined accounting.

The manuscript appears unfinished: Figures 2 and 3 are explicitly captioned “Dummy,” Figure 1 contains unrelated or unexplained labels such as “Schrodinger Bridge” and generators/discriminators not described in the method, and its caption does not explain the proposed architecture. Several related-work citations appear as missing placeholders.

Clarity is poor throughout, with pervasive grammatical errors, malformed equations and notation, unclear architectural descriptions, and claims that do not match the tables. These issues materially obstruct verification rather than being merely stylistic.

Evaluation is restricted to clean English VCTK data, with no second dataset, noisy or real-world inputs, unseen-domain evaluation, or robustness analysis. This is inadequate evidence for the paper's broad claims about natural speech reconstruction and deployment.

No code, trained models, audio samples, or sufficiently detailed implementation specification are provided. Combined with the missing losses and data splits, the results are not reproducible. The manuscript requires fundamental reconstruction and a complete, controlled reevaluation before it can support a Findings-level contribution.

strengths: Speech bandwidth extension is a relevant speech-processing problem, and using nonlinear-dynamics summaries as adversarial supervision is a potentially interesting research direction.
The paper attempts broad evaluation with spectral, intelligibility, distortion, perceptual-quality, efficiency, and architectural-ablation measurements.
The authors acknowledge important limitations, including evaluation on only VCTK, clean conditions, and one language.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are contradicted by the paper's own results. In Table 3, NDSI-BWE is worse than AP-BWE on most reported LSD, PESQ, SI-SDR, and SI-SNR comparisons, despite the text claiming superiority in LSD, PESQ, NISQA-MOS, and STOI across all three ranges.

The manuscript is materially incomplete and internally inconsistent. Figure 1 depicts an apparently unrelated Schrödinger-bridge system, Figures 2 and 3 are explicitly captioned “Dummy,” several baseline rows in Table 3 contain few or no results, and the related-work section contains unresolved citation placeholders. These issues are visible in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/26b3f30a979b4a46bbabe64db747f8fa/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The claimed method changes across sections. The abstract announces seven discriminators, including recurrence, Poincaré-plot, and multi-period components, whereas the method defines only MRLD, MSDFA, MRAD, and MRPD; MRAD and MRPD are adopted from prior work, and MPD appears only as a comparator. The claimed “four new discriminators” and novelty are therefore unsupported.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper does not specify speaker-disjoint training, validation, and test splits; utterance counts; random seeds; adversarial and reconstruction loss functions or weights; checkpoint selection; ConformerNeXt dimensions; or complete discriminator definitions. Critical MRLD parameters d, τ, and Δ and MSDFA parameters such as S and detrending order are left undefined, with no code or audio release identified.

The nonlinear-dynamics interpretation is not validated. There is no evidence that the speech segments satisfy assumptions required for estimating deterministic chaos, no reliability analysis of Lyapunov estimates on very short windows, no direct evaluation of recovered chaotic or fractal properties, and no demonstration that improvements arise from those properties rather than generic handcrafted statistics.

The proposed features raise unresolved optimization concerns. Nearest-neighbor selection in MRLD is discrete, while MSDFA appears to tile a scalar F(n) into a constant image; the manuscript does not explain meaningful gradient propagation through these operations or why a five-layer CNN over tiled constants is appropriate.

The evaluation protocol is insufficient to support the reported improvements: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated runs, or consistent controlled comparisons. Baseline training and evaluation procedures are unspecified, making the partial Table 3 results uninterpretable. Possible train/test speaker leakage cannot be excluded.

The abstract claims subjective testing with five judges, but the paper supplies no listening-test design, participant information, stimuli, rating protocol, statistical analysis, or subjective results. NISQA-MOS is a learned objective estimate and cannot substitute for the claimed human evaluation.

Several efficiency claims conflict: the abstract states an eightfold parameter reduction, the main comparison is roughly 2.1-fold against AP-BWE, and the 40-fold figure applies only to selected discriminators. RTF lacks measurement details, and discriminator costs are not clearly separated between training and inference.

Some metrics are used without adequate methodological qualification, including PESQ for 48-kHz outputs. The required resampling or metric mode is not reported, and unusually high nonintrusive NISQA scores are treated as decisive without human validation.

The writing contains pervasive grammatical errors, malformed statements, overstated causal conclusions, and inconsistent numerical interpretations. Together with the placeholder figures and incomplete tables, this prevents reliable assessment of the intended system.

Although the topic is adjacent to ACL's speech scope, the present submission is principally an audio signal-processing study and does not articulate a broader computational-linguistics contribution. More importantly, the unsupported and contradictory evidence prevents even a Findings-level soundness recommendation; fundamental reconstruction and fresh, controlled experimentation are required.

strengths: The idea of incorporating Lyapunov- and detrended-fluctuation-derived signals into adversarial speech bandwidth extension is interesting and relevant to speech processing.
The paper evaluates several bandwidth-extension ranges with multiple spectral, intelligibility, distortion, perceptual, and efficiency metrics.
The discriminator and generator ablations are useful in intent, and the proposed configuration offers a comparatively compact 33.5M-parameter generator.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is contradicted by Table 3: NDSI-BWE is worse than AP-BWE on LSD in all three ranges, PESQ in two ranges, and SI-SDR/SI-SNR throughout. Most entries for NU-Wave, EBEN, AERO, and MS-BWE are blank, so the claimed comprehensive baseline comparison cannot be assessed.

The claimed subjective evaluation with five judges is not reported: there is no protocol, participant information, rating scale, sample count, statistical analysis, or result table. NISQA-MOS is a model-based objective estimate and cannot substitute for human evaluation.

The nonlinear-dynamics interpretation is insufficiently validated. Improvements from alternative discriminator inputs do not establish that the generated speech reproduces deterministic chaos or fractal structure. No direct dynamical measurements, capacity-matched controls, significance tests, or analysis separating the proposed representation from architectural effects are provided.

The method is internally inconsistent and incomplete. The abstract introduces MRLD, MS-RD, MSDFA, MR-PPD, MPD, MRAD, and MRPD, whereas the method details only MRLD, MSDFA, MRAD, and MRPD. Critical quantities such as embedding dimension, delay, prediction horizon, tiling size, adversarial objectives, loss weights, STFT settings, and full layer configurations are unspecified.

Experimental reproducibility is inadequate: speaker-disjoint training/validation/test splits, utterance counts, random seeds, checkpoint selection, input segment duration, preprocessing details, and code availability are missing. Results from only VCTK in clean conditions also provide limited evidence of generalization.

The manuscript is visibly unfinished: Figures 2 and 3 are captioned “Dummy,” several citations appear as “?”, the main architecture caption does not meaningfully describe the figure, and numerous grammatical and typesetting problems impede interpretation. These issues, together with the unsupported empirical claims, require substantial reconstruction beyond a routine next-cycle revision.

strengths: The paper explores an interesting direction: using nonlinear-dynamics-derived statistics as adversarial signals for speech bandwidth extension. Combining Lyapunov- and DFA-inspired critics with magnitude/phase discrimination is potentially useful beyond the specific architecture studied.
The empirical evaluation covers several bandwidth settings and a reasonably broad collection of spectral, intelligibility, perceptual, distortion, efficiency, and human-evaluation measures.

The proposed system is substantially smaller than AP-BWE and obtains modest improvements on several perceptual metrics. The paper also provides layer-level parameter breakdowns, preprocessing details, software versions, and many training hyperparameters.
The authors include extensive architectural and discriminator experiments, acknowledge the single-dataset/noise-free limitation, and discuss possible misuse.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim—that the improvements arise from modeling deterministic chaos—is not adequately validated. The paper never measures whether reconstructed speech more faithfully matches ground-truth Lyapunov spectra, DFA exponents, recurrence behavior, or chaotic segments. Consequently, the experiments support at most the usefulness of additional handcrafted discriminator inputs, not the stronger chaos-based explanation.

The proposed statistics are insufficiently and sometimes incorrectly specified. MRLD omits essential choices such as embedding dimension, delay, prediction horizon, neighbor-selection rule, temporal exclusion, normalization, and handling of very short windows; reliable Lyapunov estimation from windows as short as 64 samples is especially questionable. Classical DFA characterizes scaling using the slope across multiple scales, whereas MSDFA appears to compute and tile individual fluctuation values. The text alternately describes five separate MSDFA critics and one stacked tensor, leaving the actual method ambiguous.

Several ablations are confounded. ConvNeXt and ConformerNeXt variants differ greatly in parameter count; the linear and Lattice variants also have unexplained size differences; and depth, head count, scale count, convolution type, and discriminator configuration change together across parts of Table 3. These comparisons cannot isolate the claimed contributions. There are also no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests.

The headline gains over AP-BWE are mixed and often small. CIS-BWE is worse on SI-SDR and SI-SNR in every reported range, while some perceptual improvements are only a few hundredths. NISQA-MOS is heavily emphasized despite being a learned proxy, and the very high or inconsistent NISQA values across tables are not analyzed.

The human study is too weak to substantiate claims of consistently or significantly better quality: it has only ten non-native-English student listeners, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and limited procedural detail. The reported preference advantage is internally inconsistent—11 percentage points in the main text versus 2% in the appendix. The appendix also claims robustness under noisy and reverberant conditions even though the study and limitations describe noise-free VCTK-derived data.

Reproducibility is below the Findings threshold. No code, checkpoints, generated audio, or exact train/test file lists are provided. Baseline retraining and evaluation protocols are unclear. Important loss weights and implementation details are absent, and the paper contradicts itself on using four GPUs versus one GPU. The main text also gives apparently invalid MRAD/MRPD resolution tuples, whereas the appendix gives different tuples.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic downsampling of one clean English corpus. There is no test on real telephony/channel degradation, unseen datasets, noise, multilingual speech, or downstream ASR/TTS performance, despite motivating the work through those NLP applications.

Overall, the compact model and preliminary results are promising, but important methodological clarification, controlled experiments, direct validation of the chaos hypothesis, statistically supported listening tests, and release-quality reproducibility are needed before the contribution meets the soundness bar for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant speech-processing problem and presents a concrete dual-stream magnitude/phase architecture with two proposed chaos-inspired discriminators.
The evaluation covers several bandwidth settings, objective quality and intelligibility metrics, model complexity, ablations, and a small listening study.
The appendix provides useful preprocessing, software, hyperparameter, and layer-level parameter information, and the paper acknowledges its single-corpus, English-only scope.

CIS-BWE is substantially smaller than AP-BWE and obtains modest improvements on several perceptual metrics, suggesting that the architecture may be practically useful even if the proposed explanation is not established.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim—that the gains arise from modeling deterministic chaos—is not validated. There is no analysis showing that the extracted quantities reliably distinguish chaotic speech dynamics, that generated speech better matches ground-truth Lyapunov or fractal properties, or that these properties mediate perceptual improvement. The ablations only show that adding particular learned critics can change downstream scores.

The proposed chaos features are insufficiently specified and methodologically questionable. MRLD omits essential delay-embedding parameters and nearest-neighbor details, and estimating Lyapunov behavior from windows as short as 64 samples is not justified. MSDFA appears to tile a scalar F(n) into a constant image rather than estimating the cross-scale DFA exponent normally used to characterize fractality. The algorithm and prose also disagree about whether scales use separate or stacked discriminators.

The main gains over AP-BWE are small for LSD, STOI, and PESQ, while CIS-BWE is worse on SI-SDR and SI-SNR. The largest claimed gain comes from NISQA-MOS, but no uncertainty, multiple-seed results, statistical tests, or analysis of possible metric bias is supplied. Consequently, the evidence does not support broad assertions of superior or more natural speech.

The listening study is too weak to resolve this concern: it has only ten non-native listeners from a narrow population, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and participants were briefed about the study outcome. It is described as a pairwise test despite presenting three systems, and the reported advantage over AP-BWE is inconsistent—11% in the main text but 2% in the appendix. Claims of statistically significant and broadly preferred improvement are therefore unsupported.

Experimental controls are inadequate. Generator comparisons substantially change parameter count, discriminator configuration, scale count, and other capacity variables, preventing clean attribution to ConformerNeXt, lattice interaction, or chaos-informed discrimination. Only one simulated, clean VCTK setting is used, with no cross-corpus, noisy, multilingual, or real-channel evaluation.

Reproducibility is incomplete: code, checkpoints, audio examples, exact speaker split, per-condition test counts, discriminator loss weights, phase-loss definitions, and crucial MRLD/MSDFA implementation choices are absent. The stated hardware configuration is also inconsistent between the main text (four GPUs) and appendix (one GPU).

Several descriptions and claims are inaccurate or overstated. The system uses ordinary real-valued processing of magnitude and phase rather than a clearly defined complex-valued neural network; lower parameter/FLOP counts do not improve reported RTF over AP-BWE; and the paper extrapolates to TTS and ASR without evaluating either downstream task.

The paper requires important methodological clarification, controlled experiments, uncertainty reporting, and a substantially more rigorous listening evaluation before its core claims can be considered sound and reproducible. These issues prevent a Findings recommendation in the present form.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant speech bandwidth-extension problem and proposes a technically interesting combination of dual-stream magnitude/phase modeling, Conformer/ConvNeXt components, and lightweight discriminator features.
The evaluation is broader than usual: several bandwidth settings, multiple objective metrics, complexity measurements, discriminator and generator ablations, and a listening study are reported.

The proposed system is substantially smaller than AP-BWE and numerically improves NISQA-MOS, PESQ, STOI, and LSD in the main comparison, although some gains are modest. The discriminator parameter breakdown also supports the claimed compactness of MRLD and MSDFA relative to MPD.

The manuscript supplies useful architectural diagrams, pseudocode, software versions, hyperparameters, and layer-level parameter counts, and it acknowledges the current single-dataset, English-only, clean-speech scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method specifically captures deterministic chaos is not adequately validated. The experiments show that the proposed discriminator features can improve selected metrics, but do not establish that the gains arise from modeling chaos rather than from additional handcrafted statistics or discriminator capacity. Controls using parameter-matched generic discriminators, shuffled features, or synthetic signals with known chaotic properties are needed.

The chaos features are insufficiently defined for reproduction or scientific interpretation. MRLD omits critical delay-embedding and nearest-neighbor parameters such as d, tau, Delta, neighbor selection, and normalization. MSDFA appears to tile each scale's scalar F(n) into a constant spatial map, making the claimed temporal feature-map interpretation questionable; the pseudocode also suggests one stacked SRD whereas the prose and parameter accounting describe five separate SRDs.

The principal comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and repeated-seed results. Several improvements over AP-BWE are very small, while CIS-BWE is worse on SI-SDR and SI-SNR, especially for 16-to-48 kHz. The paper therefore overstates consistent superiority and does not establish that metric differences exceed training or test-set variance.

The subjective evaluation has serious internal inconsistencies. Figure 4's legend and pie chart appear to assign only 7% preference to the proposed system, conflicting with the claim that it wins by 11%. The appendix instead claims only a 2% improvement. With ten non-native listeners, no confidence intervals or statistical tests, and results pooled across substantially different bandwidth conditions, claims of significant and broad listener preference are unsupported.

Evaluation validity and split hygiene need clarification. The exact speaker and utterance splits are not provided, no validation set is described despite extensive architecture selection, and baseline training or checkpoint procedures are unspecified. The reported 88,329 recordings also appears inconsistent with the stated VCTK composition unless augmented or paired examples are being counted. These omissions raise concerns about test-set model selection and fair baseline comparison.

The use of PESQ for 48-kHz outputs is unexplained even though standard PESQ operates at 8 or 16 kHz; any resampling and evaluation protocol must be specified. Likewise, the paper claims performance under noisy and reverberant conditions in the appendix despite describing noise-free bandwidth-limited inputs.

Reproducibility remains below the Findings threshold: code, trained models, generated audio, exact data lists, baseline configurations, several loss weights, and complete feature algorithms are unavailable. There are also configuration contradictions, including four GPUs in the main text versus one GPU in the appendix.

Overall, the model may provide a useful engineering improvement, but the evidence currently does not support its defining chaos-based explanation or several headline perceptual claims. Correcting the listening-test reporting, fully specifying and releasing the implementation, and rerunning controlled, statistically supported evaluations constitute important revisions suitable for resubmission.
